# rasuvaeff/understudy

Test double library for PHP 8.3 - 8.5 with a call-closure API.

## Install

```bash
composer require --dev rasuvaeff/understudy
```

Namespace: `Rasuvaeff\Understudy`. Requires PHP 8.3 - 8.5 and `ext-tokenizer`.
No runtime deps; `ext-mbstring` is not needed.

## Rules

- A call is specified by making it inside a closure, never by a method-name
  string: `when(fn () => $repo->find(123))`.
- The closure must contain **exactly one** direct call on a double. Anything
  else raises `InvalidCallSpecification`.
- A double exposes nothing beyond its contract. All operations are static
  methods on `Understudy`, or the free functions `when()` / `expect()` /
  `expectSequence()` / `verify()`.
- Interfaces and classes. A class may be the first target only (PHP has single
  inheritance); interfaces follow it. The target's constructor and destructor
  never run, private and static methods are left alone, protected ones are
  dispatched but unconfigurable, a writable public property keeps a declared
  default and otherwise starts empty -- including one PROMOTED through the
  constructor, which is skipped, so it differs from the real object -- and a
  `clone` is a double of its own.
- Refused before generation, each with the reason: a `final` class, a class with
  a non-private `final` instance method, an enum, a trait, an internal class, an
  anonymous class, a class that is not the first target.
- An abstract hooked property (PHP 8.4+: an interface property, or an
  `abstract` one on a class) is rendered: the generated class declares it with
  the dispatcher inside the hook. Exactly the declared hooks; a get-only
  property refuses a write with PHP's own error. A read answers the forwarding
  target's value, else what the code under test wrote (`{ get; set; }` behaves
  like a plain property), else the same default table as method returns
  (`defaults()` registrations, depth-1 nested double). A property read is NOT
  a call: not recorded, not specifiable, not judged by strict mode — the
  "exactly one direct call" rule is about calls, and reads are invisible to
  it. Still refused: a readonly class target carrying an abstract hook, and a
  `&get` hook. A concrete hook on a class target stays inherited.
- Parameter defaults are reproduced, not approximated. An object default is
  rendered from its own source expression — `new Foo(1)` and `[new Foo(1)]`
  alike — which is never evaluated during generation. Refusal is narrow: a
  default whose source names `self`, `static` or `parent` (they would resolve
  against the generated class), or an object value with no source form to
  render. A default is never silently replaced with `null`.
- `Understudy::forwarding($double, $real)` delegates every unmatched call to
  `$real` and records it. `$real` must satisfy every contract of the double.
  `Understudy::forwarding($double)` only turns the mode on for a double built by
  `Understudy::for($real)`. Configured calls still win; an expectation that only
  counts still forwards.
- `Understudy::delegate(Contract::class, $real)` is `for()` + `forwarding()` in
  one expression and returns the double. The target is validated the same way.
- `Invocation::callOriginal()` delegates one call from inside `answers()`,
  whatever the mode. Without a target it raises `OriginalCallUnavailable` — the
  parent implementation is never reached, because the double's constructor never
  ran.
- Forwarding records the boundary call only: a real method calling itself is not
  visible. A fluent method that returned the real instance comes back as the
  double; a `static` method returning another instance of the real class raises
  `OriginalReturnTypeViolation`.
- `Understudy::bypassFinals(FinalX::class)` lifts `final` off one class before
  it loads; `Understudy::bypassFinals()` does it for every class the process
  loads from then on. Opt-in, and order-dependent: it works only for classes not
  yet read from disk. `final` on methods is never lifted, so a class carrying one
  is still refused. Not available for a PHAR or a preloaded class: that source
  never passes through `file://`. A warm opcode cache does not reseal a
  bypassed class; whether the file lands in the cache at all differs by
  platform and is not something to rely on. When a class is still final
  at `for()`, the refusal distinguishes bypass never enabled, enabled for other
  classes but not this one, and enabled but out of reach.
- `Understudy::defaults(Contract::class, fn () => $value)` says what a loose
  default should be. Nearest registration wins by distance in the type graph;
  an equal-distance tie raises `AmbiguousDefaultFactory`, a wrong-typed result
  raises `InvalidDefaultValue`. Per context, dropped by `reset()`. It outranks
  `null` on a nullable return: `?Book` answers with the registered Book, and
  is `null` only when nothing was registered for it.
- Without a registration, a doublable return type becomes a double of its own,
  one level deep, adopted into the context that owns the outer double.
- `Understudy::wire(Sut::class, $overrides)` returns
  `array{sut: object, doubles: array<string, object>}`. It reads the constructor
  only. Object parameters become doubles; a nullable object still does; an
  intersection becomes one double of both; a union of several object types, a
  scalar without a default, and a by-reference parameter are refused. A variadic
  tail is left empty unless an override fills it, which takes a list and checks
  every element against the declared type. Overrides replace by parameter name
  and are not repeated in `doubles`. Every refusal happens before the constructor
  runs. Filling a variadic tail passes the parameters before it positionally, so
  an omitted optional one has its declared default materialized.
- A method declared `&method()` returns a reference into a stable per-double,
  per-method slot, so a mutation through it survives to the next read. The slot
  is seeded by the mode's own answer and then kept; a configured answer replaces
  it, a loose default does not.
- `Invocation::args` is what the call received; `Invocation::argsAfter()` is what
  the arguments became once it was answered, and is null unless the method has a
  by-reference parameter.
- A `clone` belongs to the context that cloned it, like anything `for()` builds:
  `__clone()` gets no reference to the original, so its owner cannot be
  recovered. Clone in the scope that will configure or verify the copy.
- Static contract methods are implemented only so the generated class is
  concrete. Calling one raises `InvalidCallSpecification`; inject an instance
  dependency instead.
- The call log retains returned values until `reset()`, which runner adapters
  call *after* `#[AfterTest]`/`tearDown()` — a returned stream is still open
  while your teardown runs. `Understudy::lean($double)` keeps invocations
  (method, args, sequence — matching, `verify()`, `transcript()`,
  `nothingElse()` unchanged) but not returned values; `returned()` then raises
  `OutcomeUnavailable`. One-way. Alternatively build and use the double inside
  `Understudy::scope()`, which drops the context before lifecycle teardown.
- `Understudy::reset()` after each test. Nothing is process-global on purpose:
  state lives per execution context and each Fiber gets its own — that is
  isolation, and it covers the recording phase, the call log and the sequence
  counter.
- Accounting is wider than isolation: `verifyAll()`, `reset()`, `idle()` and
  `checkpoint()` span EVERY context still holding doubles, not just the
  caller's. A test body run in a Fiber owns a context the adapter never stands
  in, and skipping it let an unmet `expect()` pass unnoticed.
- A failure message renders an object argument as `App\Book#1 {title: 'Dune'}`.
  The `#N` is an alias numbered within that one message in order of first
  appearance — never an object id, which is reused after a collection — so the
  same instance keeps one number and a rebuilt copy gets another. The braces
  list public properties only, up to five: no getter is called to render a
  message, and an object with nothing public renders as its alias alone.
- A strict double's refusal names the call and everything configured for that
  method that did not accept it, with each rejecting argument marked from the
  expectation's side — including a position the call never carried. Up to five,
  then a count. With nothing configured for the method there is nothing to
  compare against, and the message stays one line.

## API

### Creating

```php
use Rasuvaeff\Understudy\Understudy;

$repo = Understudy::for(BookRepository::class);                  // returns BookRepository
$both = Understudy::for(BookRepository::class, Countable::class); // several interfaces
$cls  = Understudy::for(DoctrineBookRepository::class);           // a class target
$spy  = Understudy::for($realInstance);                           // wraps it, does not delegate yet
```

`for(class-string<T> $target, class-string ...$interfaces): T`

For several interfaces, parameters are widened contravariantly, returns use the
narrowest compatible declaration or a synthesised interface intersection, and
parameter names come from the first (primary) interface so named arguments are
deterministic.

### Stubbing — `when()`

`when()` returns a `WhenBuilder<TReturn>`; each of its methods returns the same
builder, so actions can be replaced while configuring.

```php
use function Rasuvaeff\Understudy\when;
use Rasuvaeff\Understudy\Arg;
use Rasuvaeff\Understudy\Invocation;

when(fn () => $repo->find(1))->returns($book);
when(fn () => $repo->find(1))->returns($first, $second);   // one per call, last repeats
when(fn () => $repo->find(1))->throws(new NotFound());
when(fn () => $repo->find(Arg::any()))->answers(
    fn (Invocation $call) => new Book((string) $call->args[0]),
);
```

Matching: most recently registered wins, earlier stubs remain as fallbacks on
argument mismatch — a matching call-count expectation keeps answering after
its count is exhausted. Register the broad stub FIRST and the specific one
after it. Arguments match by `===`, or by matcher.

### Matchers — `Arg`

| Matcher | Matches |
|---|---|
| `any()` | anything, including null |
| `int(min:, max:)` | an `int` in range; a numeric string does not match |
| `float(min:, max:)` | a `float` in range; an `int` does not match |
| `string(matches:)` | a string, optionally against a PCRE pattern |
| `bool()` | a boolean |
| `same($v)` | strict identity; for objects the same instance |
| `not($v)` | negates a literal or another matcher |
| `allOf(...)` | everything every operand accepts; an operand is a matcher or a literal |
| `anyOf(...)` | anything at least one operand accepts |
| `instanceOf($class)` | an instance of the class or interface; a name that is not loadable is refused, not silently never-matching |
| `satisfies($fn, $description)` | whatever the predicate accepts |
| `containing($entries)` | an array holding these entries and possibly more |
| `count(minimum:, maximum:)` | an array or `Countable` of that size |
| `which($method, $value)` | an object whose getter answers this value |
| `none()` | an empty variadic tail; last argument only |
| `remaining()` | the whole variadic tail, any length; last argument only |
| `rest()` | declared parameters left unspelled; last argument only — the one matcher that lets a specification pass fewer arguments than the method requires: `when(fn () => $s->recordOutcome('svc', Arg::rest()))`. Stopping early without it is refused |

Every `Arg::*` returns `mixed`, so passing one where the contract says `int`
is not a type error in an IDE. `which()` calls only a public, non-static
method needing no arguments; anything else, including a getter that throws, is
a mismatch rather than an error — but a predicate handed to `satisfies()` is
the test's own code, so an exception in it travels. A matcher that could never
match is refused at construction with `InvalidCallSpecification`: an inverted
range (`int`/`float`/`count`) and a pattern PCRE cannot compile. A matcher that
reaches a real call raises `MatcherLeaked`.

`Arg::captor(?class-string $class = null): Captor` builds a typed argument
captor — the replacement for reading `args[N]` out of the call log:

```php
$options = Arg::captor(DeliveryOptions::class);   // Captor<DeliveryOptions>
when(fn () => $store->temporaryUrl(Arg::any(), Arg::any(), $options->capture()))
    ->returns('https://…');
$subject->run();
$options->last();   // DeliveryOptions, typed; NothingCaptured when empty
$options->all();    // list<DeliveryOptions>, in call order
```

`capture()` matches like `instanceOf($class)` (untyped: like `any()`); the
value is recorded only once the whole specification matched. Works in
`when()`, `expect()` and `verify()` (a `verify()` captures from the calls it
claimed, on success only); in an `expectSequence()` step it matches but does
not record. Captured values are dropped with the context —
`reset()`, a closing `scope()` — and the captor is then empty again.

### Expecting — `expect()`

`expect()` returns an `ExpectBuilder<TReturn>`, which extends
`WhenBuilder<TReturn>` and adds `ordered()`.

```php
use function Rasuvaeff\Understudy\expect;

expect(fn () => $repo->save($book));                 // exactly once
expect(fn () => $repo->count())->times(2);           // exactly twice
expect(fn () => $repo->count())->times(1, 3);        // a range
expect(fn () => $repo->count())->times(1, null);     // no upper bound
expect(fn () => $repo->find(1))->returns($book);     // behaviour too

Understudy::verifyAll();                             // checks them all
Understudy::verifyAll(strictStubs: true);            // and unused stubs
```

`expect()` is a claim about how often a call happens, checked by
`verifyAll()`. A plain `when()` stub is permission rather than a claim, and
becomes checkable only through `times()`.

A stub and an expectation for the exact same call do not stack: both orders
are refused at registration with `ConflictingExpectation`. Combine behaviour
and count in one registration — `expect(...)->returns(...)` or
`when(...)->times(n)` — and declare a repeated count once with `times()`.
A broad stub under a narrower expectation (overlap, not equality) still
composes as documented.

An expectation without an action still answers: counting and answering are
separate concerns, so `expect(fn () => $repo->count())` is complete on its own
and the mode's type-safe default supplies the value. A matched expectation
also satisfies a strict double — the call was expected.

Pest declares its own global `expect()`. Import this one as
`use function Rasuvaeff\Understudy\expect as expectCall;`, or call
`Understudy::expect()`.

`Cardinality` is the immutable call-count value object. Its factories are
`exactly()`, `atLeast()`, `between()`, `any()`, and `never()`; `allows()` tests
a count and `describe()` renders it for diagnostics.

### Chaining behaviour — `then()`

```php
when(fn () => $breaker->call($operation))
    ->returns('ok')
    ->then()->throws(new ConnectionLost())
    ->then()->answers(fn (Invocation $i) => 'recovered');
```

One link per call; the last link keeps answering after the chain runs out.
A verb without `then()` refines the same link rather than adding one.

### Verifying — `verify()`

```php
use function Rasuvaeff\Understudy\verify;

verify(fn () => $repo->save($book));                  // at least once
verify(fn () => $repo->save($book), times: 2);        // exactly
verify(fn () => $repo->save($book), minimum: 2);      // lower bound only
verify(fn () => $repo->save($book), maximum: 5);
verify(fn () => $repo->ping(), never: true);

Understudy::unused($repo);                            // no calls at all
```

### The ledger — has everything been described?

```php
Understudy::nothingElse($repo);      // every call was accounted for
Understudy::nothingElse($repo, $clock, $mailer);  // across several doubles
Understudy::allVerified($repo);      // expectations met AND nothing else
Understudy::verifySequence(          // the exact protocol, across doubles
    fn () => $repo->begin(),
    fn () => $repo->save($book),
    fn () => $repo->commit(),
);
```

A call is *accounted for* when an `expect()` matched it or a **successful**
`verify()` claimed it. A `when()` stub accounts for nothing — it is
permission, not a description. A failed `verify()` accounts for nothing
either.

`expect(...)->ordered()` requires the ordered expectations to be satisfied in
declaration order relative to each other; unrelated calls may happen in
between. `allVerified()` checks ordering as well. `verifySequence()` is the
tool when the whole protocol matters; it compares double identity in addition
to method and arguments.

```php
Understudy::expectSequence(          // armed BEFORE the subject runs
    fn () => $repo->begin(),
    fn () => $repo->save($book),
    fn () => $repo->commit(),
);

$service->handle($command);          // fails HERE, on the call out of turn
```

`expectSequence()` is the fail-fast form: both tools above raise in teardown,
where the stack trace points at `verifyAll()`. Rules, all of them load-bearing:

- Totality is scoped to the doubles the protocol names. A double it never names
  is invisible to it.
- On a named double a call must be the step due, or match something the test
  configured. Anything else is refused at the call — so a query the subject
  makes between two steps has to be stubbed with `when()`.
- Each step is due exactly once, in order. Re-calling a step the protocol has
  moved past is out of turn. Use `ordered()` for a relative order that tolerates
  repeats.
- Arming is also a claim: `verifyAll()` reports the steps the subject never
  reached, which is what still fails the test when the subject swallows the
  refusal in a broad `catch`.
- One protocol at a time; a finished one may be replaced. `checkpoint()`
  verifies it and then drops it.
- The failure is a `VerificationFailed` carrying `FailureKind::OutOfSequence`,
  the same kind `verifySequence()` reports.

### Phases and scopes

```php
Understudy::checkpoint();            // verify, then forget what is settled
$result = Understudy::scope(fn () => ...);   // nested context, verified on success
Understudy::transcript($repo);       // every call and outcome, for reading
Understudy::idle();                  // true when the test holds no doubles, in any context
```

`scope()` returns whatever the callback returns and drops its context either
way; a failure inside the callback is never replaced by a teardown error. On
success it verifies the context it opened and only that one — the enclosing
context is still running, and its open claims are answered for by
`verifyAll()`, `checkpoint()` and the runner adapter's teardown. A double
created there becomes forgotten when the scope closes. Configuration
and verification require the owning context; normal calls from another Fiber
are allowed and are routed to the owner's log.
`checkpoint()` keeps the understudies, their modes and their labels, and
clears the expectations and the SETTLED calls of the current phase — settled
meaning claimed by a matching `expect()` or a successful `verify()`. A call
covered by a `when()` stub alone is never claimed and survives, because
`nothingElse()` still reads it.

`transcript()` retains every invocation until `reset()` (see `checkpoint()`
above: it clears only the settled ones); avoid unbounded hot loops through
doubles when arguments or results hold large object graphs.

Failure raises `VerificationFailed`, whose message names the double, the
expectation, the actual count, and marks differing arguments with `*`.

### Call log — `calls()` and `lastCall()`

```php
$calls = Understudy::calls(fn () => $repo->find(Arg::any())); // list<Invocation>
$last  = Understudy::lastCall(fn () => $repo->find(Arg::any())); // ?Invocation
```

`Invocation`: `->method`, `->args`, `->sequence`, `->didReturn()`,
`->didThrow()`, `->returned()`, `->thrown()`. Its outcome is held as an
`Outcome`, built by `Outcome::returnedValue()` / `Outcome::thrownError()`.

`returned()` on a call that threw raises `OutcomeUnavailable` — `null` is a
valid return value and cannot signal "nothing".

`lastCall()` answers the newest matching call or null — the null-safe
replacement for `count($calls) - 1`, which static analysis reads as
`int<-1, max>`.

### Retiring a double — `forget()`

```php
Understudy::forget($replaced);
```

For a double the test built and then replaced: verification (including
`strictStubs`), accounting and reset stop seeing it. Any call on it — or any
question about its calls — raises `ForgottenDouble` naming `forget()`.
One-way; a replacement is a different object.

### Modes and naming

```php
Understudy::strict($repo);                   // unmatched call fails immediately
Understudy::label($repo, 'primary cache');   // name it in failure messages
Understudy::reset();                         // drop the current context
```

Loose (default) answers with a type-safe default: `null` for `void`/`mixed`/
nullable, `false`, `0`, `0.0`, `''`, `[]`, `new stdClass()`, an empty
`Generator`, an `EmptyIterator`, a no-op callable. A type with no safe default
raises `NoDefaultValue`; a `never` method raises `NeverMethodCalled`. A method
declared `: static` answers with the double itself; `: self` names the contract
and answers with a nested double.

### Exceptions

All implement `Rasuvaeff\Understudy\Exception\UnderstudyError`.

| Exception | Raised when |
|---|---|
| `InvalidCallSpecification` | the closure made no call, or threw first |
| `InvalidSpecificationArgument` | an argument no run could act on: `times(5, 2)`, a negative count, `returns()` with nothing to return, `Arg::instanceOf()` naming a class that is not loadable. Extends `\InvalidArgumentException`, which is what these paths threw before they implemented `UnderstudyError` |
| `UnsupportedTarget` | target missing, undoublable, or targets conflict |
| `StrictModeViolation` | a strict double got an unconfigured call |
| `NoDefaultValue` | loose mode has no safe value for the return type |
| `NeverMethodCalled` | a `: never` method was called without a configured throw |
| `OutcomeUnavailable` | `returned()` asked of a call that threw |
| `MatcherLeaked` | a matcher was passed to a real call, not a specification |
| `NothingCaptured` | `Captor::last()` read before any matched call captured a value |
| `ConflictingExpectation` | a when() and an expect() name the exact same call — they would not compose |
| `ForgottenDouble` | a double outlived the context that created it |
| `ContextOwnershipViolation` | configuration or verification used a double from another context |
| `AmbiguousDefaultFactory` | two registered factories are equally close to the requested type |
| `InvalidDefaultValue` | a registered factory produced something the contract cannot hold |
| `CannotWire` | the subject cannot be built, or a constructor parameter cannot be decided |
| `BypassUnavailable` | `bypassFinals()` on a loaded class, a non-class, or over another source transformer |
| `ForwardingTargetMismatch` | the instance offered to `forwarding()` misses a contract of the double |
| `OriginalCallUnavailable` | forwarding or `callOriginal()` with no real instance to delegate to |
| `OriginalReturnTypeViolation` | a forwarded `static` method returned another instance of the real class |
| `VerificationFailed` | a verification about the tested code failed |

### Structured failures — `failures()`

```php
try {
    Understudy::verifyAll();
} catch (VerificationFailed $e) {
    foreach ($e->failures() as $failure) {
        $failure->kind;             // FailureKind::UnmetExpectation | StrictStubUnused
                                    // | OutOfOrder | OutOfSequence | UnaccountedCalls
                                    // | UnusedDouble
        $failure->double;           // label of the double
        $failure->expectation;      // call spec, e.g. 'find(1)'
        $failure->expectedMinimum;  // claimed lower bound, or null
        $failure->expectedMaximum;  // claimed upper bound (null = unbounded), or null
        $failure->actualCount;
        $failure->observedCalls;    // list<Invocation> the report shows
        $failure->expectedCalls;    // OutOfSequence only: the specified protocol
        $failure->summary;          // this failure's rendered text
    }
}
```

The readonly fields of `VerificationFailure`/`FailureKind` are frozen public
API from v0.1.0 — renaming, removing or retyping one is a major-version
change. New kinds and newly-populated fields are additive.

## Not supported

Static method mocking, patching at the point of use, deep stubs, duck doubles,
sharing state across processes.
